title: Jacob's Dream at Bethel
overview: Jacob, running from his brother's anger, sleeps alone in the open and dreams of God promising to stay with him wherever he goes.

parts.label: Isaac sends Jacob away (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: After the stolen blessing of chapter 27, Jacob has to leave home, partly to escape Esau and partly to find a wife among his mother's relatives rather than the local Canaanite peoples. Isaac now knowingly passes on to him God's old promise to Abraham of many descendants and a land of their own.

parts.label: Esau tries to please his father (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: Seeing that his Canaanite wives upset his parents, Esau adds a wife from the family of Ishmael, who was also Abraham's son. Many readers see this as a late, partial attempt to win back his father's favor, since Ishmael's line was not the one the promise passed through.

parts.label: A stairway to heaven (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Alone at night with a stone for a pillow, Jacob dreams of a stairway or ramp linking earth and heaven, with angels going up and down; some scholars compare it to the stepped temple towers of the region. Christians later read this in light of Jesus, who in John's Gospel speaks of angels ascending and descending on himself.

parts.label: God's promise to Jacob (vv. 13-15)
parts.note: God names himself as the God of Abraham and Isaac and repeats their promise of land, many descendants, and a blessing for all peoples. He adds a personal promise to this lonely runaway: I am with you, I will protect you, and I will bring you back.

parts.label: This is the house of God (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: Jacob wakes in awe, realizing God was present in a place that looked like nowhere special. He stands his stone up as a marker and pours oil on it to set it apart as sacred, renaming the spot Bethel, which means "house of God."

parts.label: Jacob's vow (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: Jacob vows that if God protects him, feeds and clothes him, and brings him home, the stone will become God's house and he will give back a tenth of all he receives. Translations differ on whether "the LORD will be my God" belongs to his conditions or to his promise.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jacob's "if" vow shows a man still bargaining with God or a genuine first step of trust, with some reading "if" as meaning "since."
think: Have you ever found that a place or moment you expected nothing from, perhaps at a low point, turned out to matter a great deal to you?
